article.title: Precision at K: Evaluating Models When You Can Act on Only a Fixed Number of Cases

paragraphs.en: Many machine-learning evaluations summarize performance across all possible thresholds, but operations often use only one narrow part of the ranking. A fraud team may review 5,000 transactions per day. A sales team may call 20,000 leads per month. A campaign may have budget for one million messages. In these settings, Precision at K asks a direct question: among the top K cases selected by the model, what fraction are actually positive? This can be more operationally relevant than a global metric such as AUC. AUC measures ranking quality across pairs of positive and negative cases over the full score range. A model can have a strong AUC yet perform poorly near the exact cutoff where capacity is exhausted. Conversely, a model optimized for the top of the list may create substantial value even if its global ranking is less impressive. Precision at K should be interpreted with the base rate. If only one percent of the population is positive and precision among the top K is ten percent, the selected group has ten times the population rate. Lift at K expresses this comparison directly. Recall at K answers a different question: what share of all positive cases is captured within the available capacity? The right balance depends on business costs. When reviews are expensive, precision may dominate. When missing a positive case is costly, recall matters more. K itself is not purely statistical; it represents budget, staffing, channel limits, or customer-contact policy. Evaluation should therefore use the same K expected in production and test stability across time. If capacity changes, teams should inspect a range of plausible K values rather than one point. Confidence intervals or repeated validation can show how noisy top-K performance is, especially when positives are rare. Ties and score calibration also deserve attention. Precision at K does not require calibrated probabilities, but expected-value decisions may. Analysts should monitor realized yield after deployment because population prevalence can shift. A model evaluation becomes more useful when it mirrors the actual action. Instead of asking only whether the model separates classes globally, ask how many valuable cases the organization will find within the number it can realistically handle. Analysts should define the population, time window, operational constraint, and decision objective before interpreting the metric.
